RQ2: What does BMU-level analysis reveal about repeated marginality, price levels and concentration that fuel-type or aggregate analysis cannot?

Study window: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025 · Generated: 2026-07-17 11:14

Figure 1. Repeated marginality among leading BMUs by active side

Figure 1. Repeated marginality among leading BMUs by active side. BMUs are ranked by their tie-adjusted share of attributed marginal weight across 50,684 valid Settlement Periods, with each period contributing a total weight of one across its co-marginal BMUs. Hatched and solid segments show bid-active and offer-active contributions, respectively, while colours identify technology. Registered capacity is shown beside each BMU. The highest-ranked battery, E_DOLLB-1, ranked 32nd and is included as a reference below the top-25 threshold; it appeared in 426 marginal periods and accounted for 0.75% of total tie-adjusted marginal weight.

What the figure measures

The figure converts the original raw-occurrence table into a consistent tie-adjusted ranking. It shows which individual units repeatedly receive attributed marginal weight, how their contributions divide between long-system bid-active and short-system offer-active periods, and whether the technology pattern seen in aggregate is reproduced by individually frequent BMUs. The separated battery reference bar permits direct comparison with the minimum share among the top 25 without treating it as a member of the ranking.

Main result. The leading 25 BMUs—3.2% of the 771 marginal BMUs—account for 35.6% of total tie-adjusted marginal weight. T_HUMR-1 is the leading unit, accounting for 2.76% of all valid Settlement Period marginal weight. The top-25 contains 18 CCGT BMUs, 5 pumped-storage BMUs and 2 biomass BMUs, but no batteries. The first battery, E_DOLLB-1, ranks 32. It was present in 426 distinct marginal Settlement Periods but accounts for 0.75% of total marginal weight after fractional tie adjustment, despite batteries' prominent aggregate technology share in RQ1.

Interpretation

Repeated marginality is concentrated among a recognisable set of CCGT, pumped-storage and biomass BMUs, while battery marginality is distributed across a wider population of individually smaller units. This is the unit-level atomisation result: a technology can be frequent in aggregate without producing many individually dominant units. The side segments also prevent repeated marginality from being treated as homogeneous; units with similar total shares may occupy very different bid-active and offer-active roles.

Method and limitations

The ranking describes attributed marginal frequency, not market power, ownership concentration or a causal effect on System Price. Tie adjustment prevents periods with several co-marginal BMUs from receiving more total weight than single-setter periods. Shares use all valid bid-active and offer-active periods as the denominator, so segment size reflects both unit recurrence and the amount of time spent in each system state. Capacity is descriptive registered capacity and is not used to scale marginal weight. Plant-family and lead-party fields are retained in Appendix A rather than added to every plotted label.

Figure 2. Concentration of global SHAP attribution by identity resolution

Figure 2. Concentration of global SHAP attribution by identity resolution. Curves show cumulative tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP after ranking side-specific features from most to least globally important. Markers identify the feature that raises cumulative coverage to at least 85%; that feature is retained, so realised coverage may slightly exceed the threshold. The boundary contains 8 of 37 technology-side features, 32 of 793 plant-family-side features and 45 of 1,133 BMU-side features.

What the figure measures

The curve measures concentration of total model attribution rather than repeated marginal frequency. A steep curve indicates that a small number of identity-side features account for most global weighted mean |SHAP|; a flatter curve indicates that importance is distributed across a wider feature population.

Main result. Fragmentation and concentration coexist. The absolute number of features required to reach 85% increases from eight at technology level to 45 at BMU level, but the BMU boundary still represents only 4.0% of the 1,133 available BMU-side features. The corresponding shares are 21.6% at technology level and 4.0% at plant-family level.

Interpretation and limitations

The 85% boundary is a transparent coverage rule, not a statistical-significance threshold. Each resolution is represented by a separately fitted identity model and a resolution-specific SHAP sample; the comparison therefore concerns attribution concentration and should not be read as equality of model performance or causal importance.

Figure 3. Resolution ladder of global importance and price direction

Figure 3. Global importance and directional interpretation across identity resolution. Within each row, the left panel ranks the eight leading side-specific features using global tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP. The right panel retains the same feature set and order and reports the tie-weighted conditional mean signed SHAP when each feature is active. Positive values are associated with predictions above the corresponding model baseline and negative values with predictions below it. Colours identify technology, while labels report distinct active Settlement Periods. Models are estimated separately at technology, plant-family and BMU resolution, so cross-resolution magnitudes are interpreted descriptively rather than as directly comparable or causal effects.

What the figure measures

The left column answers which features matter most to fitted predictions overall. The right column then answers whether those already selected features are associated with predictions above or below their model baseline when active. Conditional extremes do not determine entry into the main figure.

Main result. Battery bid and offer rank fifth and sixth at technology level, yet the highest-ranked battery feature falls to rank 32 at plant-family level and rank 69 at BMU level. Broad technology importance therefore fragments across battery identities, while the leading family and BMU features instead identify particular CCGT, pumped-storage, biomass and wind actors with distinct directional associations.

Interpretation and limitations

Global mean |SHAP| is the importance criterion; conditional signed SHAP supplies direction for that fixed set. Here, n is the number of distinct Settlement Periods in the resolution-specific SHAP sample in which the feature was active; technology indicators are binary at technology–Settlement Period level, while conditional means use the model's tie weights. Neither statistic is causal. Absolute SHAP magnitudes are interpreted within each separately fitted resolution-specific model rather than as directly comparable effects across rows. The defensible comparison concerns which identities enter, their ordering and direction. The full top-20 charts, 85% qualifier tables and separately selected conditional extremes remain in the SHAP evidence-bank report.

Figure 4. BMU-level attribution and repeated marginality by active side

Figure 4. BMU-level attribution and repeated marginality by active side. Each panel contains the ten BMU-side features with the largest global tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP within the corresponding active side, ordered from most to least important. Horizontal position reports the tie-weighted conditional mean signed SHAP when the feature is active, relative to the BMU-model baseline. Colours identify technology, while marker area represents each BMU's tie-adjusted share of marginal weight within that side. Global importance determines feature selection and ordering; signed SHAP is used only to interpret the direction and magnitude of the selected associations.

What the figure measures

The figure separates three analytically different BMU-level quantities. Global mean |SHAP| determines which units enter each panel, conditional signed SHAP shows whether those selected features are associated with predictions above or below the model baseline when active, and marker area indicates how frequently the BMU receives tie-adjusted marginal weight on that side. Separating bid-active and offer-active units prevents the expected side-level sign pattern from obscuring which individual BMUs stand out within each regime.

Main result. T_DRAXX-1 is the leading globally important bid-active BMU feature and has a conditional signed association of -36.2 £/MWh. T_RYHPS-1 leads the offer-active ranking, with a conditional association of +57.1 £/MWh. The selected panels contain 0 battery BMU features, reinforcing the contrast between batteries' prominent technology-level importance and their weaker representation among the most important individual-unit features.

Interpretation and limitations

The plot identifies model associations, not causal price effects or market power. Marker area and SHAP magnitude need not move together: a BMU can be repeatedly marginal without strongly changing fitted predictions, or can have a large conditional association based on relatively few active observations. Conditional signed values use the BMU model's tie weights, while marginal-share markers use the complete 2023–2025 attributed marginal sample. The support counts, plant families, lead parties and exact values are retained in Appendix D.

Figure 5. Repeated marginality and global BMU attribution

Figure 5. Repeated marginality and global BMU attribution. Each point represents a side-specific BMU feature active at least once in the BMU-level SHAP sample. The horizontal axis reports the BMU's tie-adjusted share of marginal weight within the corresponding active side, while the vertical axis reports the feature's global tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP across the full BMU-model SHAP sample. Both axes use logarithmic scales. All plotted values are strictly positive and no plotting offset is added; features with zero mean absolute SHAP or no active SHAP-sample observation are omitted. Colours identify technology and marker area represents registered capacity, capped at 1,500 MW. Dashed lines mark the side-specific 75th percentiles of marginal frequency and global attribution; these provide descriptive reference boundaries rather than statistical classifications. Labels identify selected importance and frequency–attribution outliers, while each panel reports Spearman's rank correlation.

What the figure measures

The scatterplot tests whether BMUs that repeatedly receive attributed marginal weight are also the units whose identities most strongly differentiate fitted System Price predictions. The upper-right region contains BMUs that are both frequent and distinctive; the lower-right identifies frequent but comparatively lower-attribution identities; and the upper-left identifies lower-frequency features with higher global attribution. Figure 4 focuses on the leading actors and their signed direction, whereas Figure 5 assesses the wider frequency–importance relationship.

Main result. Frequency and model attribution are related but not equivalent. Their rank correlation is 0.38 for bid-active BMU features and 0.79 for offer-active features. Frequent-but-routine examples include T_MRWD-1, T_SEAB-1, while less-frequent but strongly attributed examples include T_FFES-3, T_WHILW-2. This is the BMU-level divergence that aggregate technology analysis cannot reveal.

Interpretation and limitations

Mean absolute SHAP is a fitted-model attribution measure, not an observed price, causal effect or test of market power. Frequency uses the complete 2023–2025 attributed marginal sample, while importance uses the BMU model's tie-weighted SHAP sample. Features absent from that SHAP sample are excluded rather than plotted as exact zeros; a printed or rounded zero would not establish that a BMU has no possible predictive role. Capacity is contextual only and does not scale either frequency or SHAP. Reference-region membership depends on descriptive 75th-percentile boundaries and should be interpreted as a visual classification.

Figure 6. Within-technology variation in BMU-level System Price distributions

Figure 6. Within-technology variation in BMU-level System Price distributions. Each row represents a BMU-side feature observed in at least 100 marginal Settlement Periods. Horizontal position is measured relative to the median System Price for the corresponding technology and active side, with zero denoting that benchmark. Thick intervals show the interquartile range, filled circles show the BMU median and thin extensions show the directionally relevant tail: P5 for bid-active periods and P95 for offer-active periods. Labels report absolute BMU medians, colours identify technology and marker area represents tie-adjusted marginal share within the active side. Technology benchmarks contain one observation per Settlement Period–technology combination, preventing multiple co-marginal BMUs of the same technology from duplicating System Price.

What the figure measures

The figure asks whether individual BMUs occupy similar conditional price distributions once both technology and active-side regime are held constant. The main-text selection contains the ten most frequently marginal supported CCGTs on each side and the leading supported battery, pumped-storage, wind, biomass and non-pumped-hydro comparator where available. It therefore contrasts recurrent BMUs without allowing the general bid–offer price difference to create an artificial within-technology spread.

Main result. Technology-level medians do not describe a single representative BMU. Even within the same technology and active-side regime, recurrent units differ in their median position, central price range and directional tail. BMU resolution therefore reveals price signatures that are concealed when observations are pooled by fuel type.

Interpretation and limitations

These are observed conditional System Price distributions, not BMU bid or offer prices, causal unit effects or evidence of market power. Differences can reflect when and where units become marginal, operational constraints, correlated system conditions and other omitted circumstances. The support rule reduces sensitivity to sparsely observed units but does not make the displayed BMUs statistically matched. The figure establishes economically material heterogeneity; attributing that heterogeneity would require a separate within-technology model or formal variance decomposition.

Appendix G. BMUs within the 85% global-SHAP coverage boundary

The BMU-resolution coverage boundary contains 45 side-specific features representing 44 unique BMUs. Of these, 14 are bid-active features and 31 are offer-active features. The selection is made by ranking all BMU-side features by global tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP and retaining the smallest leading set whose cumulative share reaches at least 85%. The crossing feature is included.

A BMU may appear twice where its bid- and offer-active indicators both qualify. The only such BMU is T_HUMR-1. Global SHAP rank and cumulative coverage refer to the combined BMU-side ranking, rather than separate within-side rankings. Conditional signed SHAP supplies direction for the selected features; it does not determine inclusion.
